content.text:
The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "Life After Death on Wikipedia": https://pudding.cool/2018/08/wiki-death
The files: data/people.csv, data/pageviews.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by exploring the data files and reading the story.

Lawrence Peter "Yogi" Berra was an American professional baseball catcher, who later took on the roles of manager and coach. He played 19 seasons in Major League Baseball (MLB), all but the last for the New York Yankees. He was an 18-time All-Star and won 10 World Series championships as a player—more than any other player in MLB history. When a famous person dies , articles are written, tweets are tweeted, and Wikipedia is
updated.
It’s a big deal.
# Life After Death on Wikipedia
What pageviews tell us about how famous people are remembered after they die.
Adjusted pageviews are the pageviews scaled to an average day of Wikipedia traffic
during the collection period of this data. The remainder of the article will refer to this simply as
“pageviews.”
= Living celebrity
But just how big? To put it in perspective, let’s look at living icon Beyoncé . Here are her
(English-language) Wikipedia pageviews between March and May of 2016, in 48-hour intervals.
On April 24, Beyoncé dropped Lemonade and the internet went wild. Her pageviews increased tenfold from about
30 thousand to nearly 300 thousand.
And now let’s take a look at Prince, starting with the period leading up to his death.
In the 48 hours after Prince’s death was reported, he accumulated over 11 million pageviews on Wikipedia.
The news of his death was reflected in the traffic.
More than 1,300 notable
people died in the past three years, according to Wikipedia. Here are 84 who got over half a million
pageviews in the first 48 hours after their deaths.
Although no one grabbed our attention quite like Prince, the spike in pageviews after a celebrity’s death
can often overshadow that of other major events, even a presidential inauguration.
While not perfect, Wikipedia traffic serves as a solid proxy for the ebb and flow of a celebrity’s cultural
relevance. It makes sense that household names like Prince and Stephen
Hawking get the most traffic immediately following their death. The bigger the star (or tragedy), the
more they are searched.
After Anthony Bourdain died, it
seemed like everybody (myself included) couldn’t talk about anything else. It was sad and unexpected.
I could rattle off a dozen other recent deaths that seemed to eclipse the rest of the news cycle. But which
celebrities’ pageviews grew abnormally high? Let’s look at the percent increase in pageviews compared
to a typical day.

The first 48 hours only tell us part of the story. We develop special relationships and often identify with
celebrities. This is why Bourdain’s death had such an impact on me. Watching his show, I traveled the world
alongside him for countless hours.
And now I rewatch him more than ever. How long celebrities remain on our radar provides a different
perspective on the impact of their death. Here are the number of weeks after death until pageviews
returned to normal.
A return to normal traffic was considered when the
pageviews fell within two standard deviations of the median of the pageviews before the date of death.
TBD means they have yet to return to normal.
Weeks until normal traffic
But not everybody’s pageviews return to normal. At the time of publishing, Bourdain’s traffic remains
steadily and significantly higher.
There are plenty of possible reasons for this; perhaps the person was relatively unknown before, and their
death increased their visibility. Or maybe there was a renewed interest in their life’s work. Let’s
look at the one-week moving average of the percent increase in pageviews compared to the pre-death
average.
Toggle annotations
Only including people with data for at least 120 days after their
death.
There are many ways to process death. For me, quantifying the public reaction offers a different way to look
at these often unexpected, tragic events.
#
Data & Methods
Data for this story were collected and processed using the Wikipedia API . The yearly aggregation of
notable deaths (e.g., 2018 ) was the
starting point. The full source and reproducible scripts are available on Github . The development of the entire
project was streamed from start to finish. Check it out on YouTube .
The period of collection was from July 1, 2015–August 1, 2018, from English Wikipedia. Only
people with at least 30 days of padding from the edge of this range, who hit 500k adjusted pageviews the 48
hours after their death, and who had a median 48-hour adjusted pageviews of 500+ before death were considered.
All pageviews were adjusted to represent traffic on an average day during this period to allow for fair
comparison across days.
A return to “normal” traffic was considered when the pageviews fell within two standard
deviations of the median before the date of death.
Get in touch with me on twitter @russellviz or by email at russell@pudding.cool.

When a famous person dies , articles are written, tweets are tweeted, and Wikipedia is
updated.
It’s a big deal.
# Life After Death on Wikipedia
What pageviews tell us about how famous people are remembered after they die.
Adjusted pageviews are the pageviews scaled to an average day of Wikipedia traffic
during the collection period of this data. The remainder of the article will refer to this simply as
“pageviews.”
= Living celebrity
But just how big? To put it in perspective, let’s look at living icon Beyoncé . Here are her
(English-language) Wikipedia pageviews between March and May of 2016, in 48-hour intervals.
On April 24, Beyoncé dropped Lemonade and the internet went wild. Her pageviews increased tenfold from about
30 thousand to nearly 300 thousand.
And now let’s take a look at Prince, starting with the period leading up to his death.
In the 48 hours after Prince’s death was reported, he accumulated over 11 million pageviews on Wikipedia.
The news of his death was reflected in the traffic.
More than 1,300 notable
people died in the past three years, according to Wikipedia. Here are 84 who got over half a million
pageviews in the first 48 hours after their deaths.
Although no one grabbed our attention quite like Prince, the spike in pageviews after a celebrity’s death
can often overshadow that of other major events, even a presidential inauguration.
While not perfect, Wikipedia traffic serves as a solid proxy for the ebb and flow of a celebrity’s cultural
relevance. It makes sense that household names like Prince and Stephen
Hawking get the most traffic immediately following their death. The bigger the star (or tragedy), the
more they are searched.
After Anthony Bourdain died, it
seemed like everybody (myself included) couldn’t talk about anything else. It was sad and unexpected.
I could rattle off a dozen other recent deaths that seemed to eclipse the rest of the news cycle. But which
celebrities’ pageviews grew abnormally high? Let’s look at the percent increase in pageviews compared
to a typical day.
Name
Avg. 48 hr. views
before death
Views 48 hrs.
after death
Increase (%)
Show More
The first 48 hours only tell us part of the story. We develop special relationships and often identify with
celebrities. This is why Bourdain’s death had such an impact on me. Watching his show, I traveled the world
alongside him for countless hours.
And now I rewatch him more than ever. How long celebrities remain on our radar provides a different
perspective on the impact of their death. Here are the number of weeks after death until pageviews
returned to normal.
A return to normal traffic was considered when the
pageviews fell within two standard deviations of the median of the pageviews before the date of death.
TBD means they have yet to return to normal.
Weeks until normal traffic
But not everybody’s pageviews return to normal. At the time of publishing, Bourdain’s traffic remains
steadily and significantly higher.
There are plenty of possible reasons for this; perhaps the person was relatively unknown before, and their
death increased their visibility. Or maybe there was a renewed interest in their life’s work. Let’s
look at the one-week moving average of the percent increase in pageviews compared to the pre-death
average.
Toggle annotations
Only including people with data for at least 120 days after their
death.
There are many ways to process death. For me, quantifying the public reaction offers a different way to look
at these often unexpected, tragic events.
#
Data & Methods
Data for this story were collected and processed using the Wikipedia API . The yearly aggregation of
notable deaths (e.g., 2018 ) was the
starting point. The full source and reproducible scripts are available on Github . The development of the entire
project was streamed from start to finish. Check it out on YouTube .
The period of collection was from July 1, 2015–August 1, 2018, from English Wikipedia. Only
people with at least 30 days of padding from the edge of this range, who hit 500k adjusted pageviews the 48
hours after their death, and who had a median 48-hour adjusted pageviews of 500+ before death were considered.
All pageviews were adjusted to represent traffic on an average day during this period to allow for fair
comparison across days.
A return to “normal” traffic was considered when the pageviews fell within two standard
deviations of the median before the date of death.

Search not helpful. Let's focus on the data.

The data likely was built for a benchmark with certain reproducible findings. We need to identify findings the data reproduces. The main candidates:

A. Prince 48h pageviews > 11 million (reproducible exactly).
B. Percent-increase ranking/table — top entries. The story table labels each row's numbers. We could write a fact computing "increase = views 48h after / avg 48h before * 100" for every person, sorted descending, and claim top rows. But the printout must agree with the story. Since the top three in data (Astori, Zhou, Tioté) are excluded from the story table due to the methods filter (before median >= 500), we should apply the story's filter first. Then the top three become Kate Spade 161,429%, Chester Bennington 160,921%, Roy Halladay 122,066%. Story: 161,427, 160,919, 122,000. Rounding differences tiny (2, 2, 66). "up to rounding" - 122,066 vs 122,000 is within 0.05%, could be rounding to nearest 1000? Hmm, the story displays exact integers for the first two. The tiny 2-unit differences come from data version. That's fine "up to rounding." But then Avicii: story 112,357 vs ours 112,358 (1 off). Fine.

However, the story table's order differs slightly: story has George Michael 77,379 vs ours 77,380; Chris Cornell 77,315 vs 77,316; fine.

Also note difference: story uses 48h views after death computed from raw 48h window but maybe not the rolling max. For people like Leonard Cohen, story table lists 29,036% (row "Canadian poet and singer-songwriter" not visible? Actually story table has "Musician, actor, record producer 19,406 5,927,572 30,546" = David Bowie. And "Leonard Cohen" maybe not visible in excerpt? We saw "Canadian..." not in excerpt. Let's list story table rows from web_view text with exact numbers and compare.

Leonard Cohen: ours before 5,835, max 1,694,242, inc 29,036. But story row "4,453 1,299,573 29,184" is R. Lee Ermey (ours 4453, 1,299,587, 29,185). Then story probably has Leonard Cohen at 29,036.

The chart's table doesn't show all; but it's consistent.

For the table finding, how to express? "The biggest percent increases in pageviews 48 hours after death were Kate Spade (161,427%), Chester Bennington (160,919%), and Roy Halladay (122,000%)." Source: chart labels: "Kate Spade ... 161,427", "Chester Bennington ... 160,919", "Roy Halladay ... 122,000". But the story's own words are chart labels, not a sentence. The requirement: source: "the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label." We could quote the column header + row? Maybe source should be e.g. "Increase (%)\nKate Spade\nAmerican fashion designer\n2,117\n3,417,416\n161,427" — that's exact from chart. Hmm.

Maybe better to focus on a single fact per specific finding. The task says each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. The table is a chart listing all rows. "When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once." So the percent-increase table is one finding: the percent increase for each person. Code computes for every person (after filter). Claim could say "Among people with a pre-death median 48-hour adjusted pageview count of at least 500, the percent increase in the first 48 hours after death ranged from 5,995% (Charles Manson) to 161,429% (Kate Spade), with Kate Spade, Chester Bennington and Roy Halladay highest." That's a claim built from printout. The printout sorted series would show all. The numbers in the claim need to be in printout. Source: quote the table header maybe "Avg. 48 hr. views before death / Views 48 hrs. after death / Increase (%)". That's not a finding statement though. Could quote "Let's look at the percent increase in pageviews compared to a typical day." plus chart labels? The source should be story's own words; maybe the sentence "But which celebrities' pageviews grew abnormally high? Let's look at the percent increase in pageviews compared to a typical day." is the finding's framing. But it doesn't state numbers. Hmm.

Alternatively, each row is a finding? But chart states same thing for each item = one finding. I think one fact for the ranking is right, with source quoting the chart labels exactly, maybe the top row's text.

- Beyoncé's pageviews increased tenfold from about 30 thousand to nearly 300 thousand (Apr 24). Not reproducible (no Beyoncé).
- Prince accumulated over 11 million pageviews in 48h after death. Reproducible.

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
v=pd.read_csv('data/pageviews.csv'); p=pd.read_csv('data/people.csv').set_index('pageid')
# choose people and compute pre stats, show post weeks
for nm in ['Jonah Lomu','John Glenn','David Cassidy','Maureen O\'Hara','Nancy Reagan','Yogi Berra','Harry Dean Stanton','Chyna','Wes Craven','Prince (musician)','Anthony Bourdain',"Dolores O'Riordan",'Kate Spade']:
    r=p[p.name==nm].iloc[0]
    d=v[v.pageid==r['name'] if False else v.pageid==r.name if False else v.pageid==p[p.name==nm].index[0]].sort_values('timestamp_index').reset_index(drop=True)
    pre=d[d.death_index<0].views_adjusted
    med=pre.median(); sd=pre.std(); lo=med-2*sd; hi=med+2*sd
    post=d[d.death_index>=0].copy()
    post['week']=post.death_index//7
    wk=post.groupby('week').views_adjusted.agg(['mean','median','min','max'])
    # first week where median <= hi and >= lo
    within=((wk['median']>=lo)&(wk['median']<=hi))
    first=within.idxmax() if within.any() else None
    print(f"{nm}: med={med:.0f} sd={sd:.0f} bounds=({lo:.0f},{hi:.0f}) first_week_median_normal={first} npost={len(post)}")
    print(wk.head(6).to_string())
    print()
EOF

The first post-death 48h window that is normal, then weeks = floor(window_start/7). We computed 48h first and got: Jonah 7→1, John 12→1, David 6→0, Maureen 11→1, Nancy 14→2, Johan 16→2, Gordie 15→2, Arnold 13→1, Fidel 14→2, David Rockefeller 13→1, Don 13→1, Glen 13→1, Jerry 18→2, Charles Manson 9→1, Jim 13→1, Shashi 23→3, Alexis 18→2, Zsa 17→2, Miguel 28→4, Chuck 18→2, Roger 22→3, Adam 24→3, Yogi 28→4, Ali 26→3, Bhumibol 33→4, Florence 41→5, Malcolm 23→3, Billy 28→4, R. Lee 24→3, Harry 34→4, Chyna 51→7, Prince 54→7.

Compare story: 
- Jonah 0 vs 1
- John 0 vs 1
- David 0 ✓
- Maureen 1 ✓
- Nancy 1 vs 2
- Johan 1 vs 2
- Gordie 1 vs 2
- Arnold 1 ✓
- Fidel 1 vs 2

- Florence 3 vs 5
- Malcolm 3 ✓
- Billy 3 vs 4
- R. Lee 3 ✓
- Harry 4 ✓
- Chyna 5 vs 7
- Prince ~8 vs 7 (annotation says couple months)

Many match! Mismatches could be due to using the wrong median/std window. The matches: David, Maureen, Arnold, David Rockefeller, Don, Glen, Manson, Jim, Alexis, Zsa, Chuck, Ali, Malcolm, R. Lee, Harry. That's a lot. Mismatches mostly story bucket lower by 1-2. Perhaps the story uses a slightly different pre-death std (maybe std of daily, not 48h) or a different median window. But direction: story earlier than ours, meaning story's bounds are wider or its comparison starts differently.

Maybe story uses std from people.csv but median from... Let's tune: using med=median_views_adjusted_before, sd=people.std; compare 48h rolling sums. We did. What if sd is computed as 2*std of daily (or people.std corresponds to daily)? For many, people.std is close to daily std? For Roddy Piper people.std 619 vs daily std 413. For Jonah people.std 6658 vs daily 3642. So people.std ~ 1.7x daily. Wider bounds -> earlier normal.

If we use daily values with bounds = median_views_before ± 2*std (people std), we got daily_half_first which uses med/2, sd/2. That's the same as 48h. Hmm.

What if "pageviews" for normal test are the *raw views* (not adjusted)? Similar.

What if the std is the IQR-based robust std? people.iqr? No.

What if the condition is "weekly average fell within two standard deviations" where standard deviation is computed from the *post-death* data? No.

Let's look at the story's chart more carefully by trying to extract the D3 data from the page. Maybe the page's JS bundle contains a JSON with week values. The web page likely loads data from a static file. Let's inspect the HTML using a browser-like fetch that returns raw body. The `web_fetch` tool seems to convert to markdown (it returns "Skip to main content...", links). It might use a readability parser. Could try appending `.json` or viewing a known data path. Let's guess the Pudding's asset structure. Many Pudding projects on GitHub are static sites deployed at pudding.cool/YYYY/MM/slug/. Data often in `assets/data/`. The HTML may reference js/main.js, data/*.csv. We can fetch `https://pudding.cool/2018/08/wiki-death/assets/data/people.csv` etc. But we need to know. Maybe `https://pudding.cool/2018/08/wiki-death/data/people.csv`? Let's try a few with web_fetch; 404 or data.

Title: Life After Death on Wikipedia
URL Source: https://pudding.cool/2018/08/wiki-death/
Markdown Content:
**When a famous person dies**, articles are written, tweets are tweeted, and Wikipedia is updated.
**It’s a big deal.**
What pageviews tell us about how famous people are remembered after they die.
While not perfect, Wikipedia traffic serves as a solid proxy for the ebb and flow of a celebrity’s cultural relevance. It makes sense that household names like [Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_(musician)) and [Stephen Hawking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Hawking) get the most traffic immediately following their death. The bigger the star (or tragedy), the more they are searched.
After [Anthony Bourdain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Bourdain) died, it seemed like everybody (myself included) couldn’t talk about anything else. It was sad and unexpected.
I could rattle off a dozen other recent deaths that seemed to eclipse the rest of the news cycle. But which celebrities’ pageviews grew abnormally high? **Let’s look at the percent increase in pageviews compared to a typical day.**

There are many ways to process death. For me, quantifying the public reaction offers a different way to look at these often unexpected, tragic events.
### **Data & Methods**
Data for this story were collected and processed using the [Wikipedia API](https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/API:Main_page). The yearly aggregation of notable deaths (e.g., [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018#Deaths)) was the starting point. The full source and reproducible scripts are available on [Github](https://github.com/the-pudding/wiki-death-data/). The development of the entire project was streamed from start to finish. Check it out on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLsuhXm2zs07JuSfrNentA3DxAbaFO7ay2).
The period of collection was from July 1, 2015–August 1, 2018, from English Wikipedia. Only people with at least 30 days of padding from the edge of this range, who hit 500k adjusted pageviews the 48 hours after their death, and who had a median 48-hour adjusted pageviews of 500+ before death were considered. All pageviews were adjusted to represent traffic on an average day during this period to allow for fair comparison across days.
A return to “normal” traffic was considered when the pageviews fell within two standard deviations of the median before the date of death.

# Wiki Death Data
“You only live as long as the last person to remember you.” - Akecheta (Westworld)
[Screencasts](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLsuhXm2zs07JuSfrNentA3DxAbaFO7ay2) of the story as it is created.
## Setup
#### Dependencies
- [node](https://nodejs.org)
- [npm-run-all CLI](https://github.com/mysticatea/npm-run-all)
#### Install
Clone the repo and run `npm i`
## Reproduce
Individual steps below, or run `make reproduce`
##### `npm run download-year-pages`
Download the HTML for the year event pages from wiki that contain a list of all notable deaths (2015-2018).
#### `npm run parse-year-pages`
Extract every person and their meta data from the event pages to create a single csv of all notable deaths from 2015-2018.
#### `npm run get-wiki-pageviews`
Use wiki pageviews api to get the daily pageviews for en.wikipedia.org so that we can calculate percent of traffic for each person and look into seasonality in the data.
#### `npm run get-people-pageviews`
Use the wiki pageviews api to get the daily pageviews for each person in our full list of notable deaths.
#### `npm run bin`
Bin each person's pageviews by multiple intervals (1 week, 72hrs, 48 hrs).
#### `npm run stats`
Calculates a bunch of summary statistics for each person (Must choose bin).
#### `npm run filter-population`
Reduces the data to people who satisfy some quantiative criteria.
#### `npm run add-details`
Gets more detail info on each person from wiki and custom spreadsheet.
#### `npm run prepare-explore`
Consolidates and optimizes data for visual exploration.
#### `npm run prepare-web`
Streamlines data for web presentation.

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
v=pd.read_csv('data/pageviews.csv'); p=pd.read_csv('data/people.csv')
def calc(nm, start=2):
    r=p[p.name==nm].iloc[0]; d=v[v.pageid==r.pageid].sort_values('death_index').set_index('death_index')
    pre=d[d.index<0].views_adjusted; med=pre.median(); sd=pre.std(); lo=med-2*sd; hi=med+2*sd
    post=d[d.index>=start].views_adjusted
    within=((post>=lo)&(post<=hi))
    f=within[within].index[0] if within.any() else None
    return f, med, sd, lo, hi

content.text:
# Development
Run `gulp` to fire up the project server.
Any changes to the `src/` folder will trigger live reload.
#### Device testing
To view local dev link on a mobile device connected to same network, update the option to `online: true` in `gulp-tasks/browser-sync.js`. Then after you run `gulp`, grab the url from the terminal and you're good to go.
## HTML
**Where it goes:** `src/html/partials/story/`.
The main HTML file is `src/html/index.hbs`. Generally speaking, You should mostly just include new partials in there and not modify too much of it since there are a bunch of presets.
Partials are not automatically included. You must add them to `index.hbs`. If you created a new file `content.hbs` it would be referenced as `{{> story/content }}`.
#### Sticky header with menu
Change `base/header` in `index.hbs`:
* `{{> base/header 'sticky' }}`
* `{{> base/header 'sticky-dark' }}`
#### Metadata
Fill out `template-data/meta.json`
#### Copy
Using a Google Doc for copy is recommended. We use [ArchieML](http://archieml.org) as a micro CMS.
**Setup Google doc**
* Create a Google Doc
* Click `Share` button -> advanced -> Change... -> to "Anyone with this link"
* In the address bar, grab the ID - eg. ...com/document/d/**1IiA5a5iCjbjOYvZVgPcjGzMy5PyfCzpPF-LnQdCdFI0**/edit
* In the file `config.json` in root of project, paste in the ID
Running `gulp fetch-google` at any point (even in new tab while server is running) will pull down the latest, and output a file `template-data/copy.json`.
You can now reference the JSON in your HTML, namespaced by `copy` (eg. ` {{copy.explanation}}
`).
#### SVG icons
There is a directory called `svg` in the root of project, it contains a bunch of [icons](https://feathericons.com/). To include them in the HTML, simply do this:
` @@include('arrow-left.svg')
`
This way you can drop in svg icons anywhere in your HTML code whilst keeping it uncluttered.
## JavaScript
**Where it goes:** `src/js/`
Take a look at `entry.js`. This is the kickoff file, the only one included and run automatically.
Then take a look at `graphic.js`, it has some basic skeleton stuff setup for you. This is imported and called from `entry.js` once on load, and subsequently on a debounced resize event. I recommend putting your code in here. If you want to create more files, I recommending doing that in `graphic.js`, but remember they won't be executed until you import them.
[D3 Jetpack](https://github.com/gka/d3-jetpack/) is included globally by default. For any other libraries, it is recommend that you use `npm` to install and import them. You can also do it the vanilla way by including them in the `src/assets` folder and putting a script tag in the HTML.
The JavaScript is transpiled from ES6, and uses Webpack to bundle into a single file. That means each file creates its own closure, so a "global" variable is scoped to a file unless you declare it as `window.variable = ....`.
#### Installing libraries
**NPM way**:
`npm install [name] --save`.
Usage: (see library docs, but usually) `import [library] from '[library]'`
**Old school**
Put JS file in the `src/assets/scripts` directory.
Usage: reference in the `index.hbs` file ` `
#### JavaScript utilties
In the folder `src/js/utils` there a are a bunch of handy helper JS functions.
* `dom.js`: Super minimial wrapper on basic vanilla dom selection for convenience and cross-browser.
* `is-mobile.js`: Device sniffing to detect if on mobile hardware.
* `load-image.js`: Async image loading to detect when image completely loaded.
* `locate.js`: Estimate user location via ip address.
* `truncate.js`: Truncate string with options to break on space and add ellipses.
* `url-parameter.js`: Get and set the paremeters of the URL in address bar.
* `lookup-state-name.js`: Get state name from state abbrevation.
* `lookup-state-abbr.js`: Get state abbrevation from state name.
* `tracker.js`: Fire simple GA tracking on events.
#### The Pudding's favorite libraries
* [d3-annotation](http://d3-annotation.susielu.com/)
* [lodash](https://lodash.com/)
* [moveto](https://github.com/hsnaydd/moveTo)
* [jump.js](http://callmecavs.com/jump.js/)
* [nouislider](https://refreshless.com/nouislider/)
* [geolib](https://github.com/manuelbieh/geolib)
* [scrollama](https://github.com/russellgoldenberg/scrollama)
* [ScrollWatch](https://edull24.github.io/ScrollWatch/)
NoUISlider is included by default, with some preset pudding styles. To include it, simply include the library in your JS file `import noUiSlider from 'nouislider'`. Then in `src/css/config.styl`, uncomment `no-ui-slider.styl`.
## CSS
**Where it goes:** `src/css/story/`.
There is a file for you to start off with, `story.styl`. You can create as many files as you want in this directory, they are automatically included.
Checkout some of the auto-included files in `src/css/utils/` (`variables.styl`, `helpers.styl`, `presets.styl`). You can modify these, especially `variables.styl`.
## Fonts
Fonts are loaded async and use the [FOUT](https://www.zachleat.com/web/comprehensive-webfonts/#fout-class) practice. We have three font families:
* **Canela** (class name: `tk-canela`)
* **Publico** (class name: `tk-publico`)
* **Atlas Grotesk** (class name: `tk-atlas`)
Simply include the class on the element, and all children will inherit it. Publico is included on the body tag by default.
Example:
```html
test
```
Use the **font-weight** CSS property. Available weights:
* Canela: 300, 700
* Publico: 400, 700
* Atlas: 400, 500, 600
## Assets
**Where it goes:** `src/assets/`
I reccommend creating separate directories for images, data, etc. Assets can always be referenced relative to `assets` directory. For example:
* ` `
* `d3.csv('assets/data/test.csv')`
When deployed, assets paths will remain relative. _However_, you'll notice that in `index.hbs` there is a line that like ` `. `basepath` here switches from nothing in local development, to `https://pudding.cool/` in production. We have a common assets folder for stuff like (which also occurs with fonts). If you need to use this project for a non-pudding one, make sure to update the `basepath` variable in `gulp-tasks/html.js`.
## Deploy
Run `gulp dist`
This generates a single html file with inlined css, a single js file, and a folder with assets in the `dist` folder.
**Update Github pages version (during development)**
Run `make github` (make sure you've enabled github pages in your repo settings to pull from `docs`).
**Update The Pudding version (launch)**
Requirements:
* [awscli](https://aws.amazon.com/cli/)
* [configure aws](http://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/configure/index.html)
* [configure cloud](http://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/cloudfront/create-invalidation.html).
In `Makefile`, replace `year/month/name` with your own (eg. `2017/01/nba`). Uncomment code.
Run `make pudding` to deploy and bust cache. If you only made changes to html/css/js, you can run `make aws-htmljs` then `make aws-cache` (it will be much quicker than re-uploading all your assets).
## Pre-launch checklist
* optimize images: make sure they aren't unncessarily large in dimensions (should be no more than 2x their final rendered dimensions), should also crunched with something like [imageoptim](https://imageoptim.com/online).
* clean data: reduce filesize bloat by making sure you aren't loading unnecessary columns and rows.
* remove console logs: aesthetics :smile:
* enable anayltics: be sure analytics partial is included (`analytics.hbs`)
* fill out metadata: `template-data/meta.json`
* create two social images:
_ Facebook: 1200 x 628 (`src/assets/social/social-facebook.jpg`)
_ Twitter: 1024 x 576 (`src/assets/social/social-twitter.jpg`)

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
v=pd.read_csv('data/pageviews.csv'); p=pd.read_csv('data/people.csv')
def week_for(pid):
    d=v[v.pageid==pid].sort_values('death_index').set_index('death_index')

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
v=pd.read_csv('data/pageviews.csv'); p=pd.read_csv('data/people.csv')
# last date per pageid and overall
v['date']=pd.to_datetime(v.timestamp.astype(str))
res=[]
for _,r in p.iterrows():
    d=v[v.pageid==r.pageid].sort_values('death_index').set_index('death_index')
    # days after death available
    n_after=(d.index>=0).sum()
    pre=d[d.index<0].views_adjusted
    med=pre.median()
    after=d[d.index>=23].views_adjusted
    if len(after)==0: continue
    ma=after.rolling(7).mean()
    diff=(ma-med)/med
    # only days bin_death_index>=30 (impact.csv filter)
    diff30=diff[after.index>=30]
    res.append((r['name'],n_after,med,diff.max(),diff30.max(),diff30.mean(),diff30.iloc[-1] if len(diff30) else np.nan))
df=pd.DataFrame(res,columns=['name','n_after','med','max_all','max30','mean30','last30'])
elig=df[df.n_after>=120]
print('eligible',len(elig))
print(elig.sort_values('max30',ascending=False).head(20).to_string(index=False))
print()
print(elig.sort_values('mean30',ascending=False).head(20).to_string(index=False))
EOF

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
v=pd.read_csv('data/pageviews.csv'); p=pd.read_csv('data/people.csv')
def week_for(pid, stat='mean'):
    d=v[v.pageid==pid].sort_values('death_index').set_index('death_index')
    pre=d[d.index<0].views_adjusted
    c=pre.mean() if stat=='mean' else pre.median()
    sd=pre.std(); lo=c-2*sd; hi=c+2*sd
    after=d[d.index>=2].views_adjusted
    within=((after>=lo)&(after<=hi))
    if not within.any(): return np.nan, np.nan
    day=within[within].index[0]
    return np.floor((day-1)/7), day
